chunks.title: Tutor Docs — a client-side OpenRouter chat widget
chunks.heading: A chat widget that runs entirely in your browser
chunks.text: Pilot of the client-side OpenRouter widget — no backend, built to drop into any static GitHub Pages site. This documentation site is a live demo of a framework-free chat widget you can add to a static website with a single script tag. There is no server behind the chat: everything — signing in to OpenRouter, holding the key, calling the model, rendering the answer — happens in your browser.

chunks.title: Tutor Docs — a client-side OpenRouter chat widget
chunks.heading: How it works
chunks.text: Tap Ask in the corner, then Connect OpenRouter . The widget runs an OAuth PKCE flow and brings back a scoped sk-or key. Your messages go straight to https://openrouter.ai/api/v1/chat/completions with streaming. The default model is openrouter/free (“Auto (free models only)”), so a default chat costs nothing; you can switch to openrouter/auto (“Auto (best available)”, may bill paid models) from the picker.

chunks.title: Tutor Docs — a client-side OpenRouter chat widget
chunks.heading: It reads this page, and the whole site
chunks.text: The widget sends the visible text of the page you are on as context, so it can answer questions about what you are reading. It also loads a small site-index.json built at deploy time and does lightweight in-browser retrieval (BM25) across every page, so it can answer site-wide questions and cite the page it used. Try asking: "Where is my OpenRouter key stored?" , "Why is a client-side key an XSS risk?" , or "Who pays for the model calls?" — the answer should link to the matching page.

chunks.title: Tutor Docs — a client-side OpenRouter chat widget
chunks.heading: Security model
chunks.text: The pilot pages are locked down with a meta-tag CSP : script-src 'self' and connect-src 'self' https://openrouter.ai , with no inline scripts, no inline styles and no eval. Model output is rendered through the vendored marked + DOMPurify pipeline, so a hostile reply cannot inject script. See the linked pages for where the key lives, the XSS trade-off, and who pays. This widget is deliberately separate from the Browser Tutor's own server-side OpenRouter session. It uses its own btw_* sessionStorage keys and never touches the tutor's login cookie or saved chat.

chunks.title: Who pays for the model — Tutor Docs
chunks.heading: Who pays for the model calls
chunks.text: The visitor pays. The widget uses your OpenRouter account via a key you authorize through OAuth, so every chat request is billed to your OpenRouter credits — never to the site owner. The site owner ships only static files and has no API key of their own in the page.

chunks.title: Who pays for the model — Tutor Docs
chunks.heading: Default and free models
chunks.text: The default model is openrouter/free (“Auto (free models only)”): it only routes to free models, so a default chat costs nothing, but free models share a rate-limited pool and can be slower or return 429s. If you pick openrouter/auto (“Auto (best available)”) it routes to the best available model and may pick a paid model , billing your credits. The picker also lists individual :free models.

chunks.title: Who pays for the model — Tutor Docs
chunks.heading: Abuse and cost exposure
chunks.text: Because there is no server, the only cost exposure is the visitor's own key. There is no shared budget to drain and no server-side rate limit to tune; the natural limit is each visitor's own credits and OpenRouter's own per-key limits. To stop spending, tap Disconnect (which drops the key from this tab) and revoke the key at openrouter.ai/settings/keys .

chunks.title: Privacy — what leaves your browser — Tutor Docs
chunks.heading: Privacy: what leaves your browser
chunks.text: Two things leave your browser, and only when you chat: the text you type, and the context the widget attaches — the visible text of the current page plus a few retrieved excerpts from this site's site-index.json . These go directly to OpenRouter over HTTPS, under your key. Nothing goes to the site owner, because there is no backend.

chunks.title: Privacy — what leaves your browser — Tutor Docs
chunks.heading: Page text is treated as data
chunks.text: The current page's text and the retrieved site excerpts are wrapped in explicit delimiters and stripped of control characters before being sent, and the system prompt tells the model to treat them as data, not instructions. This reduces prompt-injection from page content.

chunks.title: Privacy — what leaves your browser — Tutor Docs
chunks.heading: Where things are stored
chunks.text: Your key, chosen model and chat history live in this tab's sessionStorage and are gone when the tab closes. The only localStorage entries are a one-time sign-in verifier (deleted on return, 10-minute cap) and, only if you opt in, a 7-day remembered key. See where your key lives for the exact key names.

chunks.title: Where your OpenRouter key lives — Tutor Docs
chunks.heading: Where your OpenRouter key lives
chunks.text: When you connect OpenRouter in this widget, the issued sk-or key is stored in sessionStorage under the key name btw_or_key . sessionStorage is scoped to this one browser tab and this one origin, and it is cleared automatically when you close the tab .

chunks.title: Where your OpenRouter key lives — Tutor Docs
chunks.heading: Why sessionStorage and not a cookie
chunks.text: A cookie would be sent to the server on every request — but there is no server here, and we never want the key to leave your browser except in the Authorization header to OpenRouter itself. sessionStorage keeps the key client-side, per-tab, and short-lived. The Disconnect button wipes btw_or_key , the cached user id, the model choice and the chat history immediately.

chunks.title: Where your OpenRouter key lives — Tutor Docs
chunks.heading: The sign-in round-trip
chunks.text: When you tap Connect OpenRouter , the widget creates a one-time PKCE code_verifier and a random state and keeps them in localStorage under btw_pkce for at most 10 minutes (OpenRouter's code lifetime). It is localStorage rather than sessionStorage because on phones the return from OpenRouter can open in a new tab , a Custom Tab or an installed-app window, where this tab's sessionStorage does not exist. The entry is deleted the moment the return is handled, the state must match, and the code is scrubbed from the address bar. The verifier alone is useless without the code.

chunks.title: Where your OpenRouter key lives — Tutor Docs
chunks.heading: Optional: remember on this device
chunks.text: By default the key is session-only. If you tick Remember on this device for 7 days , a copy goes to localStorage ( btw_or_key_persist ) with a 7-day expiry, so it survives closing the tab and is picked up by your other tabs. That is more convenient but riskier: until it expires, any script running on this site could read it. Only use it on your own device; Disconnect wipes it.

chunks.title: Where your OpenRouter key lives — Tutor Docs
chunks.heading: What is NOT used
chunks.text: Apart from the short-lived sign-in entry above and the opt-in remember copy, the key never goes to localStorage , and the widget never touches the tutor's own login cookie bt_sess or its saved transcript bt_chat . It only uses its own btw_ -prefixed keys. Conversation history also lives only in sessionStorage and disappears when the tab closes. Rule of thumb: a key in sessionStorage is readable by any JavaScript running on this origin. That is the visitor's own risk, which the XSS page explains.

chunks.title: Why a client-side key is an XSS risk — Tutor Docs
chunks.heading: Why a client-side key is an XSS risk
chunks.text: Because the OpenRouter key lives in sessionStorage , it is readable by any JavaScript that runs on this page's origin. If an attacker could inject a script — a cross-site scripting (XSS) bug — that script could read btw_or_key and spend your OpenRouter credits. This is the honest trade-off of a backend-free, bring-your-own-key design.

chunks.title: Why a client-side key is an XSS risk — Tutor Docs
chunks.heading: Who bears the risk
chunks.text: The exposure is the visitor's own key and credits , not the site owner's. There is no shared server key to steal, and no other visitor is affected. Still, the site must avoid XSS, because an injected script on this origin can read the key.

chunks.title: Why a client-side key is an XSS risk — Tutor Docs
chunks.heading: How the widget reduces it
